title: Achilles: the heel and invulnerability
subtitle: The glory and the weak point
subject: mythologie
description: Achilles, hero of the Iliad, seems invincible. A heel, an arrow, and the myth invents the universal metaphor of the fatal weak point.

hero.hook: Troy's greatest warrior. Almost impenetrable skin. And a heel that changes the meaning of the word “weakness”.

blocks.text: **Achilles** is the central hero of the **Iliad**, Homer's poem about the Trojan War. Son of the nymph **Thétis** and the mortal **Peleus**, he embodies the perfect warrior: fast, fierce, obsessed with , the glory that survives after death. [[Kleos]]
Its story combines quasi-divine power and certain mortality. A detail of the body, the heel, has become the universal symbol of the flaw hidden at the heart of strength.

A prophecy announces that Achilles will be more powerful than his father. **Zeus** and **Poseidon** therefore renounce Thetis and marry her to Peleus. To protect the child, Thétis immerses him in the **Styx**, a river of Hell whose water would make the skin impenetrable.

blocks.caption: Thetis plunges Achilles into the Styx, holding him by the heel.

blocks.text: This magical version of invulnerability appears late, in the poet  (1st century). In Homer, Achilles is not protected by a spell: he is simply the best fighter, and therefore always mortal. [[Stace]]
She holds him by the **heel**. This area remains dry, therefore vulnerable. The technical detail becomes the heart of the myth.

Before Troy, Achilles withdraws from the fight after an affront from **Agamemnon**, leader of the Greeks, who takes his captive . Without him, the Achaean army collapsed. It was the death of **Patroclus**, his dearest companion, which brought him back to the front. [[Briseis]]

blocks.caption: Achilles facing Hector, decisive duel under the walls of Troy.

blocks.text: He dons armor forged by, blacksmith god, and launches a [[Hephaestus]], a series of extraordinary warrior exploits. He kills **Hector**, prince of Troy, then drags his body behind his chariot. This, this proud excess, is shocking. Only the nocturnal visit of the old king **Priam** brings Achilles back to humanity: he finally returns the body for the funeral. [[aristia]] [[Hubris]]
Achilles would have had a choice: a long and forgotten life, or a short and forever famous life. He chooses glory. This choice defines Greek tragic heroism.

Under the walls of Troy, **Pâris**, prince archer little esteemed for his bravery, shoots an arrow. Guided by **Apollo**, the projectile reaches the Achilles heel. The greatest warrior falls by the least valiant of fighters.

blocks.caption: The death of Achilles: the arrow of Paris hits the heel.

blocks.text: His ashes are mixed with those of Patroclus. Even dead, Achilles remains an issue: people argue over his weapons. The era of heroes begins to close.

The expression “**Achilles heel**” still refers today to the flaw in an apparently solid system. In anatomy, the [[Achilles tendon]] recalls the same myth. In politics, IT or strategy, the idea remains the same: nothing is stronger than its weakest link.
Beyond the metaphor, Achilles embodies the Greek dilemma: live a long time in the shadows, or shine little and remain immortal in the stories. By choosing to fight, he gained literary immortality.
Almost invulnerable thanks to the Styx, Achilles dies at Troy from an arrow in the heel. The myth leaves to posterity the [[Achilles tendon]] and the universal image of the fatal weak point.
